passage:
Counsellor's note, Monday.
Tenzin from Class 10 died suddenly over the weekend. This morning his class made a memorial board outside their room, and I sat with them. Some wrote cards and cried quietly. Alka refused to join; she stood at the window with her arms folded and said, “A board won't bring him back.” Rohan could not stop talking, telling story after story about Tenzin's cricket until his own voice shook. Several pinned a card without a word and left. One boy asked me quietly whether he should have been nicer to Tenzin. I told the class there is no wrong way to feel and no right one, and that my room is open to anyone who wants to talk. Parents were informed today. I spoke to Alka alone at lunch and will call home this afternoon.
Disha, school counsellor

qa.q: What did Tenzin's class make outside their room?
qa.a: They made a memorial board and pinned cards on it.

qa.q: What might Alka have been feeling when she refused to join and said, “A board won't bring him back”?
qa.a: Alka may have been angry and deeply hurt, so the board felt too small for the loss; refusing to join can be one way of grieving.

qa.q: What did Disha do to support the class?
qa.a: Disha sat with the class, said there is no wrong way to feel, kept the counsellor's room open, informed parents the same day and spoke to Alka alone before calling home.

qa.q: What might Rohan have been going through while telling story after story about Tenzin?
qa.a: Rohan may have been holding on to happy memories to keep the shock away, until it caught up and his voice shook. 🤍

grounding: Students react differently after a classmate's sudden death, some crying, some refusing, some talking non-stop, some feeling guilty, and a counsellor accepts every reaction.

passage:
Pallavi's diary, Wednesday night.
The whole school was silent in assembly today because of Neha. Some girls cried so hard they had to be taken out. Jomon kept cracking jokes in the corridor afterwards, and I got so angry that I told him to stop. He looked at me strangely and walked away. Later I saw him sitting on the back steps, not saying anything. I felt terrible. I don't think the jokes mean he doesn't care. I didn't cry at all today, and I felt guilty about that too, as if I'm doing it wrong. Mum said grieving has no correct way, and Ms Iyer said the counsellor is there for all of us. Tomorrow I'll sit with Jomon on the steps.
Pallavi

qa.q: Where did Pallavi see Jomon sitting later?
qa.a: Pallavi saw Jomon sitting on the back steps, not saying anything.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling after not crying all day?
qa.a: Pallavi felt guilty, as if grieving the wrong way, and also sorry for snapping at Jomon.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do tomorrow about feeling guilty and about Jomon?
qa.a: Pallavi could sit with Jomon on the steps without pushing him to talk, and could speak to the counsellor about the guilt of not crying.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Pallavi told him to stop?
qa.a: Jomon may have felt hurt or misunderstood, which fits the strange look and walking away to sit alone.

grounding: A school loses a student and students grieve differently, some crying, some joking and some silent, and none of it is wrong.

passage:
Diary, Thursday.
Tenzin from 10C died on Sunday in a bike accident. The assembly today was the quietest I've ever heard our school. Some girls were sobbing. Some boys at the back were making jokes, and I felt so angry at them, until Jaya said her cousin laughed at their grandfather's funeral and then cried for a week.
I didn't cry at all. I just felt blank, and then guilty for feeling blank. I sat behind Tenzin in the computer lab and never really spoke to him. Now I keep thinking I should have.
The counsellor said everyone grieves differently and her door is open. Jaya and I are going to go tomorrow at lunch, together.
Sunaina

qa.q: How did Tenzin die?
qa.a: In a bike accident on Sunday.

qa.q: What is Sunaina feeling after the assembly?
qa.a: Sunaina feels blank, then guilty about feeling blank, and regretful about never really speaking to Tenzin.

qa.q: What helpful next step has Sunaina planned?
qa.a: Going to the counsellor with Jaya at lunch tomorrow, instead of carrying the guilt alone.

qa.q: How does Jaya help Sunaina see the boys who joked differently?
qa.a: By sharing that her cousin laughed at a funeral and cried for a week after, showing that jokes can be a way of grieving too.

grounding: A school loses a student; one teenager feels blank and guilty while others cry or joke, and none of it is wrong.

passage: When the news came that Rajesh from their class had died of dengue during the monsoon holidays, the small school in Mandya felt different. The headmaster held a two-minute silence under the neem tree. Some girls cried openly; a few boys kicked stones and joked about the bus being late. Farhan didn't cry or joke. He sat on the steps where he and Rajesh used to share groundnuts and didn't move till the bell. His friend Karthik, who couldn't sit still, got the class to collect notebooks for Rajesh's little sister. That evening, the class teacher found Farhan still on the steps and sat down beside him without saying anything. After a while, Farhan said, 'He owed me two rupees.' Then his face crumpled.

qa.q: What did Karthik get the class to collect?
qa.a: Notebooks for Rajesh's little sister.

qa.q: What does Farhan's line about the two rupees show?
qa.a: Farhan had been holding his grief in silence, and a small, ordinary memory finally let the sadness break through.

qa.q: What did the class teacher do that helped Farhan?
qa.a: The teacher sat beside him quietly without pushing him to talk, giving him room to grieve in his own way.

qa.q: Why might Karthik have thrown himself into collecting notebooks?
qa.a: Keeping busy and doing something useful may be Karthik's way of grieving, since he couldn't sit still.

grounding: A small-town school grieves a classmate; students cry, joke, stay silent or keep busy, and each is a way of grieving.

passage: The news came on Tuesday morning in the school hall in Utrecht: Jonas from 10B had died in a cycling accident at the weekend. Nobody moved. Then Leila began to cry, loudly, into her sleeve. Two boys at the back cracked a joke and laughed too hard, then went red. Emil just stared at the floor. He kept thinking of the pencil Jonas had lent him in September, still in his case, and that he had never said thanks. At lunch the canteen was strangely polite. Someone snapped at the jokers, "Have some respect." The counsellor, Ms de Vries, spoke quietly to the tables. "People grieve in different ways. Crying, joking, going silent. None of that is wrong. My door is open all week." Emil went on Thursday, holding the pencil.

qa.q: What had Jonas lent Emil in September?
qa.a: Jonas had lent him a pencil in September.

qa.q: Why did Emil keep thinking about the pencil?
qa.a: He felt guilty and sad that he had never said thanks, and the pencil made the loss feel personal.

qa.q: How did Ms de Vries support a school grieving in so many ways?
qa.a: She said openly that crying, joking and silence are all normal, and offered an open door all week, so students like Emil could come when ready.

qa.q: Why might the two boys at the back have laughed too hard?
qa.a: They were probably shocked and awkward, and the laughter was a nervous way of coping, which is why they went red afterwards.

grounding: Shows a whole school hit by a classmate's death, with students crying, joking or going silent, and none of it treated as wrong.
